summary: Provides Path Computation Element Communication Protocol extensions for stateful PCE to support point-to-multipoint TE LSPs. The PCE is an appropriate technology for computing such paths. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: One sender wants to reach many receivers. This lets a central planner work out and manage the tree of paths.

questions: what is stateful pce for p2mp
what are pcep p2mp capability flags
subtitle: How a central path computer can build and manage one-to-many MPLS tunnels over PCEP.

tldr.problem: PCEP already let a stateful Path Computation Element manage point-to-point tunnels, but a point-to-multipoint tree has many leaves, so messages are large and changes to one leaf should not require resending the whole tree.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8623 adds capability flags, a P2MP flag in the LSP object, a P2MP-LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV, a new S2LS object and message fragmentation, and reuses the PCRpt, PCUpd, PCReq, PCRep and PCInitiate messages for trees.
tldr.outcome: A stateful PCE can create, update, report on, grow, prune and delete P2MP TE LSPs, referring to each tree by its PLSP-ID. It is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 9756 updates it.

today: RFC 8623 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) is an entity that can compute a network path or route from a network graph and a set of constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) asks a PCE for paths. RFC 5440 defines the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) for point-to-point (P2P) path computation, and RFC 8306 extends it to ask for paths for point-to-multipoint (P2MP) TE LSPs.

RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 added stateful PCE and PCE-initiated LSPs for P2P tunnels. RFC 8623 complements that work by defining what a stateful PCE needs in order to support P2MP TE LSPs. It describes setup, maintenance and teardown of PCE-initiated P2MP LSPs.
sections.eli5: There was already a planner that could manage single routes from A to B. This document teaches it to manage routes from one place to many places.

sections.title: Why Stateful PCE for P2MP
sections.content:
The use cases in RFC 8051, such as optimization and recovery, apply equally to P2MP TE LSPs. There is also a size argument. With a stateless PCE, a request to modify an existing P2MP tree must present all the leaves along with all the path information.

With a stateful PCE, messages can use the PCEP-specific LSP identifier (PLSP-ID) to stand for everything already exchanged about the LSP. Only the modifications, such as new or removed leaves, need to be encoded. The PLSP-ID indexes the LSP database at the PCE and identifies the LSP at the PCC.

The ability for a PCE to trigger creation of P2MP TE LSPs on demand also fits a controller-based network where the controller decides when and where to set up paths.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending the whole map every time, you give the tree a name tag. Then you can just say, "add this house to tree number 5."

sections.title: Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
PCEP speakers advertise stateful capability in the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV of the OPEN object. This document adds three one-bit flags to it. Each must be advertised by both the PCC and the PCE before the related messages are allowed on the session.

  • N (P2MP-CAPABILITY): allows P2MP extensions of PCRpt state reports.
  • M (P2MP-LSP-UPDATE-CAPABILITY): allows P2MP extensions of PCUpd messages.
  • P (P2MP-LSP-INSTANTIATION-CAPABILITY): required on both sides for PCE-initiated P2MP LSP instantiation.

For discovery through OSPF or IS-IS, the PCE-CAP-FLAGS sub-TLV gets three new bits: 13 (Active Stateful PCE with P2MP), 14 (Passive Stateful PCE with P2MP) and 15 (PCE-Initiation with P2MP). Advertising in the IGP does not replace advertising in PCEP at session setup.

Using the extensions without having advertised the capability is an error. For example, a PCC that understands the extensions but did not advertise them SHOULD answer a PCUpd with a PCErr (error-type 19, error-value 12) and terminate the session.
sections.eli5: Before they start, both sides hold up cards saying what they can do. They only use a trick if both cards show it.

sections.title: Extended PCEP Messages
sections.content:
The message formats are written in Routing Backus-Naur Format. The extended messages are:

  • PCRpt: a PCC reports the state of a P2MP TE LSP. At least one END-POINTS object MUST be present, and an S2LS object MUST accompany it.
  • PCUpd: a PCE updates the attributes of a P2MP TE LSP. The END-POINTS object MUST be carried.
  • PCInitiate: a PCE asks a PCC to create or delete a P2MP TE LSP. The END-POINTS object MUST be carried for instantiation.
  • PCReq and PCRep: a PCC or PCE MAY include the LSP object once the stateful P2MP capability is negotiated.

The P2MP END-POINTS object from RFC 8306 lists leaves grouped by leaf type: 1 adds new leaves, 2 removes old leaves, 3 marks old leaves whose path can be modified or reoptimized, and 4 marks old leaves whose path must be left unchanged. When reporting, leaves with the same leaf type and the same operational status are grouped together. Leaf type 3 is used for delegated LSPs and leaf type 4 for nondelegated ones.
sections.eli5: The messages are the same envelopes as before, but now each one has a list of destinations, and each destination is marked as new, removed, changeable or leave-alone.

sections.title: New Flags, TLV and Object
sections.content:
Three flags are added to the LSP object: N (the message is for a P2MP TE LSP), F (the LSP is fragmented and this is not the last piece) and E (the route is in compressed format, using SERO and SRRO objects). They apply to PCRpt, PCUpd and PCInitiate; in PCReq and PCRep they have no meaning and MUST be ignored.

Two P2MP-LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLVs identify a tree, one for IPv4 (type 32, length 16) and one for IPv6 (type 33, length 40). They carry the tunnel sender address, LSP ID, Tunnel ID, Extended Tunnel ID and P2MP ID. The TLV MUST be in the LSP object of a PCRpt for a P2MP LSP, MAY be in a PCUpd (all zeros means all paths of that PLSP-ID), and SHOULD NOT be in a PCInitiate because the PCC generates the identifiers and reports them back.

The new S2LS (Source-to-Leaves) object, object class 41 and object type 1, reports the state of a group of leaves from an END-POINTS object. Its 3-bit O field is the operational status of that group, while the O field in the LSP object covers the whole tree. A conflict between them triggers error-type 10, error-value 22.
sections.eli5: The new name tag has the sender's address and a few ID numbers. The S2LS note says which group of houses is working and which is not.

sections.title: Adding Leaves, Fragmentation and Errors
sections.content:
Instantiation and deletion of P2MP TE LSPs work as in RFC 8281. To delete, the PCE sends a PCInitiate with the PLSP-ID of the LSP and an SRP object with the R flag set. Adding and pruning leaves of a PCE-initiated tree MUST be carried in a PCUpd, using leaf type 1 to add and leaf type 2 to prune. The PCC MAY use the Incremental State Update mechanism of RFC 4875 to signal this.

A PCEP message can be at most (2^16)-1 bytes, so a large report, update or initiate request may not fit. The sender sets the F flag on every piece but the last, and all pieces share the same PLSP-ID (for PCInitiate, PLSP-ID 0 and the same SRP-ID-number). Missing the last piece is reported with error-type 18 and error-value 2 (report), 3 (update) or 4 (instantiation).

Other new errors: error-type 6 with error-value 13 for a missing S2LS object and 14 for a missing P2MP-LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV.
sections.eli5: If the list is too long for one envelope, you split it across several and mark all but the last as "more coming."

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Stateful operations on P2MP TE LSPs are more CPU intensive and use more bandwidth than for P2P TE LSPs. A rogue PCC that could request unauthorized operations might mount a denial-of-service attack on a PCE. An attacker might also flood a PCC with PCUpd messages by spoofing messages or compromising the PCE.

As in RFC 8231, it is RECOMMENDED that these extensions only be activated on authenticated and encrypted sessions between PCEs and PCCs of the same administrative authority, using TLS as in RFC 8253. Other security considerations are inherited from RFC 8306, RFC 8231 and RFC 5440.
sections.eli5: Big shared plans are expensive to handle, so a trickster could overload the planner. Keep the conversation private and only between trusted parties.
